Photograph: James Veysey/Rex/Shutterstock Budget deficit UK borrows £18bn in August, putting pressure on Healey before budget Higher-than-expected figure will make chancellor’s aim of calming jittery bond markets more difficult Business live – latest updates Phillip Inman Tue 22 Sep 2026 03.16 EDT First published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK government borrowed a higher-than-expected £18.3bn last month, increasing the pressure on John Healey as he attempts to calm jittery bond markets before next month’s budget. Official figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Tuesday said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £2.9bn higher last month than in August 2025. It meant that borrowing was £3.5bn higher than expected by the government’s independent forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), taking the deficit over the financial year so far to £77.3bn – £8.1bn above forecast. The £18.3bn borrowed in August was also more than the £15.6bn City analysts had forecast. UK government borrowing jumps over forecast to £18.3bn in August as ‘fiscal straightjacket’ tightens – business live Read more Healey, the chancellor, has promised to stick within the government’s spending limits, which restrict the amount the Treasury can borrow as a proportion of national income. The August figures come after the government ran a larger-than-expected £1.8bn deficit in July , when analysts had expected the figure to be zero. The UK has been among the countries hardest hit by the rise in the interest rate on government bonds amid turmoil in financial markets . UK borrowing chart While the cost of financing UK bonds has eased in the last week, the Treasury remains under pressure to show it can reduce its reliance on heavy borrowing to maintain welfare spending. On Tuesday, the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds rose three basis points (bps) to 5.232%, while 30-year bond yields were also 3bps higher at 5.729% in early trading. Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, said: “The PM and chancellor will be feeling quite claustrophobic today as the walls close in around them. Borrowing costs keep climbing, while borrowing itself is outpacing the teeny rise in tax receipts.” The Institute for Fiscal Studies, a thinktank, said that since April, the government had spent £50bn on debt interest, £2bn more than forecast by the OBR in March. “On those forecasts – made before the most recent hikes in government interest rates – debt interest was set to be more than £100bn every year over the next five years,” said Nick Ridpath, an IFS research economist. Central government spending on social security benefits and pensions climbed by almost £10bn more than in the same period last year – from £135.3bn to £145bn – mostly in response to rising inflation. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The consumer prices index rose last month to 3.1% and, while the Bank of England held interest rates at its latest meeting last week, the central bank warned that the cost of borrowing may need to rise in the coming months if inflationary pressures persist. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI Strategy, said: “Today’s public finance figures are another unwelcome setback for the government ahead of next month’s budget.” The International Monetary Fund has urged western governments to gain greater control over their public finances to reassure financial markets that they remain safe havens for lenders. Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was committed to improving the UK’s economic growth, “but we can only deliver that growth with fiscal discipline”. She added: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.” The Conservative party Treasury spokesperson, Andrew Griffith, accused Labour of losing control of the public finances. “They are borrowing so much they’ve overshot the OBR forecast by an extra £8bn of debt,” he said. “It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to both have the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.” However, the OBR has said estimates of government borrowing published early in the financial year should be considered provisional and they are likely to be revised. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/un-a.text: Unul dintre emisarii preşedintelui american Donald Trump pentru soluţionarea negociată a războiului din Ucraina, Jared Kushner, care este şi ginerele său, a afirmat luni că se înregistrează progrese în direcţia unui acord care să pună capăt acestui conflict, deşi există în continuare provocări semnificative. Într-o postare pe reţeaua socială X, Kushner a menţionat că el şi celălalt emisar american, Steve Witkoff, au avut noi discuţii cu Iuri Uşakov, consilierul de politică externă al preşedintelui rus Vladimir Putin, asupra următorilor paşi în procesul de negociere. El a adăugat că au avut de asemenea o discuţie productivă cu Ucraina şi cu partenerii europeni. „Facem progrese, în strânsă coordonare cu Rusia, Ucraina şi Europa, către un rezultat care poate pune capăt acestui război, care poate consolida securitatea europeană şi crea bazele unei păci durabile”, a scris Kushner în mesajul său, potrivit AFP, preluată de Agerpres. Totuşi, „rămân provocări importante, iar un acord final va necesita decizii dificile”, a avertizat emisarul SUA. Setarile tale privind cookie-urile nu permit afisarea continutul din aceasta sectiune. Poti actualiza setarile modulelor coookie direct din browser sau de aici – e nevoie sa accepti cookie-urile social media El a adăugat că ultimele discuţii s-au referit şi la modalităţile de a facilita un dialog direct între Europa şi Rusia. „Este important ca ambele părţi să-şi asculte reciproc preocupările şi propunerile, în timp ce noi lucrăm în direcţia unui viitor mai stabil şi mai sigur pentru Europa”, a concluzionat Jared Kushner. Preşedintele ucrainean Volodimir Zelenski a afirmat şi el că negociatorii desemnaţi de aliaţii europeni ai Ucrainei au avut o primă discuţie cu emisarii ucraineni şi americani asupra viitoarelor negocieri cu Rusia pentru încheierea războiului, discuţie despre care a spus că „nu a fost uşoară”, dar că a condus la „un rezultat”, pe care nu l-a precizat. De partea sa, Kremlinul a reafirmat luni, printr-o declaraţie a consilierului prezidenţial Iuri Uşakov, că următoarea rundă de negocieri, la o dată încă neprecizată, se va desfăşura tot în formatul tripartit Rusia-Ucraina-SUA, fără aliaţii europeni ai Ucrainei, a căror prezenţă la masa negocierilor este respinsă în continuare de Rusia. La rândul său, şefa diplomaţiei europene, Kaja Kallas, a semnalat după o reuniune a miniştrilor europeni de externe că aliaţii europeni ai Ucrainei îşi menţin poziţia de a fi convenită o încetare a focului în Ucraina „înainte de a discuta orice altceva”, în timp ce Rusia refuză orice armistiţiu în timpul procesului de negociere. Mai mult, a adăugat Kallas, statele UE nu doresc să discute despre o nouă arhitectură de securitate în Europa, a temă impusă de Rusia în aceste negocieri. „Nu avem nevoie de o nouă arhitectură de securitate.
